1275.title: Everyday mysticism
1275.hook: Karl Rahner said the Christian of the future would be a mystic or nothing
1275.tomorrow: For the life of the world
1275.howItsDone: Some Christians end the day by looking back for where God was present in ordinary events, a practice known in Jesuit spirituality as the examen; others speak of practicing the presence of God in daily work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thomas Merton: a monk who found the crowd at the end of the silence. Your line was contemplation is for all.

Who counts as a mystic? Saints with visions. Hermits in caves. People who seem to float a little above the rest of us. Karl Rahner, a German Jesuit priest and theologian, gave a different answer. He's remembered for saying, in effect, that the Christian of the future will be a mystic, or will not be anything at all. That sounds like an impossibly high bar, until you hear what he meant by mystic. A new week starts here, in an ordinary place.

For Rahner, a mystic isn't someone with visions. He means someone who has actually experienced God, not only heard about God secondhand. Faith that rests on custom alone, he thought, would struggle in a world where custom no longer carries people along. So where would ordinary people meet God? Not mainly in rare moments, Rahner said, but inside daily life. Keeping silent when you've been wronged and could defend yourself. Forgiving when no one will thank you for it. Doing what your conscience asks when no one will ever know. Staying faithful in a task that brings no reward and no feeling of glory. In moments like that, he said, a person may be touching the Spirit at work, even if it feels like nothing at all. The letter to the Colossians, speaking about ordinary household work, says something close: "And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men." If that's so, the kitchen, the commute and the office aren't outside God. Rahner's name for this was a mysticism of everyday life. Not a ladder out of the ordinary. A way down into it. Others have said it in their own words. Brother Lawrence, the Carmelite lay brother this path met earlier, worked in the kitchen and spoke of practicing the presence of God among the pots and pans. The vocabulary differs, and the direction is the same: the plain moment may be the place.
screen: `A MYSTIC: ONE WHO HAS EXPERIENCED GOD.`
`NOT A LADDER OUT, A WAY IN.`

segments.voice: Look back over the last day for one ordinary moment that held something more: a time you held your tongue, a kindness nobody saw, a task finished well with no one watching. Don't judge whether it counts; just stay with it and notice what was there. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for that moment; if you don't, simply let it be noticed.
Everyday mysticism. Karl Rahner's idea that God can be met inside daily life itself: in silence, in forgiveness, in faithfulness no one sees.
Your line: mystic in the ordinary. No visions required, just a plain moment. Rest well.

1276.title: For the life of the world
1276.word: For the life of the world
1276.hook: Alexander Schmemann: humans are priests of creation, offering the world back in thanks
1276.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians gather for the Divine Liturgy, whose center is the Eucharist, and Christians in many churches say grace before meals in many forms, from a set prayer to a few words of thanks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Karl Rahner: God met in plain moments nobody sees. Your line was mystic in the ordinary.

Before a meal, some families go quiet for a moment. A hand reaches for another hand. Someone says a few words of thanks, and then the dishes are passed and the noise comes back. Alexander Schmemann, an Orthodox priest and teacher, thought that small pause was a key to the whole of life. He wrote a short book about it, and he took its title from the Gospel of John: For the Life of the World.

Schmemann starts with something basic. People are hungry. We eat to live, and we stay hungry for more than food. In Genesis, he notices, the world first comes to humans as something to eat: a garden full of fruit, given as a gift, and God sees that it's good. So what are humans for? Schmemann's answer: we are the ones who can bless. Every creature eats. Humans can receive the world, give thanks to God for it, and offer it back. He calls this the priestly role of every person: a priest of creation. Not a job title. A way of holding things. When the thanks goes missing, the world doesn't stop being good. We just start treating it as stuff to use up. That's where the title comes in. In John, Jesus says: "the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world." At the heart of Orthodox worship is the Divine Liturgy, and at its heart is the Eucharist, a Greek word meaning thanksgiving. Christians understand what happens at that table in different ways, as this path has seen, and it ranks none of them. For Schmemann, the Eucharist shows what all of life is meant to be: received, blessed, offered back. The first letter to Timothy says it plainly: "every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving." So grace before a meal isn't a pause before real life. In Schmemann's eyes, it's real life in miniature, at a kitchen table.

If there's something near you to eat or drink, a glass of water, an apple, a cup of coffee, look at it and think about where it came from: the soil, the rain, the long road it traveled to reach you. If you pray, you can say a grace you already know, slowly, or thank God in your own words; if you don't, let the thanks rise anyway, to whoever it reaches.
For the life of the world. Alexander Schmemann's book, and his picture of humans as priests of creation, receiving the world and offering it back to God in thanks.

1277.title: Liberation theology
1277.hook: Gustavo Gutiérrez read the gospel from the side of the poor
1277.howItsDone: In some Catholic and Protestant communities, small groups read the Bible together in light of their own lives and act on what they read; churches also speak of a preferential option for the poor in their social teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Alexander Schmemann: humans as priests of creation, giving the world back in thanks. Your line was the world as sacrament.

In a poor neighborhood of Lima, in Peru, a Catholic priest named Gustavo Gutiérrez spent his days among families who had very little. One question kept pressing on him: how do you tell people who are poor, and pushed aside, that God loves them? Not in theory. On their street, with their hunger. Out of that question came a book, A Theology of Liberation, and a movement that came to share its name. Its starting point was simple to say: read the gospel from the side of the poor.
screen: `HOW DO YOU SAY GOD LOVES YOU?`
`READ FROM THE SIDE OF THE POOR.`

segments.voice: Luke tells a scene in Nazareth. Jesus stands up in the synagogue, unrolls the scroll of Isaiah, and reads words this path met earlier in Isaiah: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor." The reading goes on, all the way to "to set at liberty them that are bruised." Then he sits down and says this scripture is fulfilled today. Gutiérrez asked: what does good news to the poor sound like to someone who is actually hungry? His answer had a few parts. First, God has a special love for the poor. Not because they're better people, he insisted, but because God is good. The phrase that grew up around this is the preferential option for the poor. Second, theology comes second. First comes commitment: living alongside people and sharing their struggle. Then you reflect on it, in the light of the word of God. Third, sin isn't only personal. It can be built into the way a society is arranged. Mary sings about God turning things over: "He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree." Liberation theology drew both praise and criticism inside the Catholic Church, including from Rome, where some worried about political readings of the gospel and borrowings from Marxist analysis. Its defenders answered that it was the gospel, read from a different chair. Christians weigh it differently. The question it leaves on the table is a plain one: whose eyes are you reading with?

Bring to mind the story of the rich man and Lazarus: a poor man laid at a rich man's gate, covered in sores, hoping for crumbs from the table. Now take Lazarus's place on the ground by the gate: what do you see from down there, who walks past, and what would good news sound like from that spot? If you pray, you can bring what you notice to God.
Liberation theology. Theology done from the side of the poor, starting with commitment, and reading the gospel as good news of freedom.
Your line: from below. The view from Lazarus's place by the gate. I'll be here tomorrow.

1278.title: Black theology
1278.hook: James Cone saw the cross in the lynching tree and God on the side of the oppressed
1278.howItsDone: In some Black churches, preaching and song hold Christ's suffering together with the community's own history, and spirituals such as "Were You There" are sung in Holy Week; Cone's books are read in seminaries and churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gustavo Gutiérrez: reading the gospel from the side of the poor. Your line was from below.

An old spiritual asks a question that seems to have no date on it: "Were you there when they crucified my Lord?" Tradition traces songs like it, the spirituals this path met earlier, to Black Christians in America, singing under slavery. James Cone grew up in Black churches in the American South, where songs like that were sung. As a theologian, he asked a question that would not leave him alone. If Jesus was a man executed on a tree, what does the cross say to people who watched their neighbors hanged from trees?

Cone's fullest answer came in a book called The Cross and the Lynching Tree. His point was plain. Rome crucified Jesus in public, as a warning, the kind of death the empire used to humiliate people it wanted to crush. Lynching in America, Cone wrote, was public too, a warning to Black communities, often with a crowd looking on. The two trees, he said, belong side by side, and he pressed the church to look at both. The New Testament itself calls the cross a tree. The first letter of Peter says that Christ "his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree." Cone read that word with American history in his ears. His second claim was about God. In Exodus, God speaks from the burning bush: "I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt, and have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows." Cone kept returning to lines like that. God sees. God hears. God takes the side of those who are crushed. That's what he meant by Black theology: the gospel heard from inside a people's suffering and their struggle to be free. And he held to Easter: the one hanged on the tree was raised. Christians read Cone in different ways. He kept coming back to the old spiritual, and to its question, which is put to every listener: were you there?
screen: `IN HIS OWN BODY ON THE TREE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one place where people are being crushed, a neighborhood, a country, a prison, or one person you know, and let it be real for a moment without rushing past. If you pray, you can hold them before the God who says, in Exodus, I have heard their cry, in your own words or in silence; if you don't, hold them in mind and ask what one small thing you could do.
Black theology. The gospel heard from inside Black suffering and struggle, with God on the side of the oppressed, and the cross standing beside the lynching tree.
Your line: the cross stands with them. God sees, and God hears. Go gently.

1279.title: Feminist and womanist voices
1279.hook: women theologians reread scripture and tradition, recovering women's voices
1279.howItsDone: Some Christians study the women of the Bible in reading groups and sermon series, and feminist and womanist theology is taught in some seminaries; churches differ on whether women are ordained.

segments.voice: Yesterday, James Cone: the cross beside the lynching tree, and God on the side of the oppressed. Your line was the cross stands with them.

A servant woman runs into the desert. She's pregnant, she's been treated harshly, and she has nowhere to go. Her name is Hagar, an Egyptian in the household of Abraham and Sarah, and this path has met her before. By a spring of water in the wilderness, the angel of the Lord finds her and speaks to her by name. Then Hagar does something startling. She gives God a name: "Thou God seest me." Her story can be read as a side scene in Abraham's. Some theologians read it as the main one.

Feminist theology is a name for rereading scripture and the Christian past with women in view. It asks: who is speaking here? Who is silent? Who got left out of the retelling? Scholars such as Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza and Rosemary Radford Ruether wrote in this way. Womanist theology grew from the experience of Black women, taking its name from a word used by the writer Alice Walker. One womanist theologian, Delores Williams, read Hagar as a mirror: a woman enslaved, used, and sent into the wilderness, and met there by God, who doesn't free her right away but helps her and her child survive. Read this way, women turn up at turning points. In Mark, when the disciples have fled, women are watching the cross from a distance. In John, Mary Magdalene meets the risen Jesus in the garden and goes to tell the disciples she has seen the Lord. Paul commends a woman he calls, in the King James spelling, Phebe, "a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea," and sends greetings to women who worked alongside him. None of this is hidden; it's on the page. Traditions differ on what these texts mean for leadership, ordination and roles. Some churches ordain women as pastors and priests; others hold that certain ministries belong to men. The method is open to anyone: read slowly, and ask whose story is also here.

Bring Hagar to mind, alone by the spring, carrying fear, exhaustion and a child on the way; hear a voice call her by name, and hear her answer, naming God as the one who sees her. If you pray, you can speak to the God who sees; if you don't, notice who in your own life goes unseen. And if you're the one being hurt or unsafe right now, please reach local emergency help, or call or text 988 in the US.
Feminist and womanist voices. Women's rereadings of scripture and tradition, recovering stories like Hagar's, and the women at the cross and the empty tomb.
Your line: her story too. Hagar named the God who sees her. See you tomorrow.

1280.title: Pentecostal theology
1280.hook: a theology of the Spirit, experience and empowerment
1280.howItsDone: Pentecostal and charismatic Christians worship with spoken and sung prayer, raised hands, testimony and prayer for healing, and pray for the gifts of the Spirit; other churches also mark the feast of Pentecost each year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, feminist and womanist voices: Hagar naming the God who sees. Your line was her story too.

A plain building on Azusa Street in Los Angeles, a place this path has visited before. People crowd in to pray, and they stay late. The preacher is a Black man named William J. Seymour. Visitors carry stories away: people speaking in tongues, people healed, Black and white worshipers praising God in the same room. Some come to mock, and some come back to stay. Pentecostals tell their story through revivals like this one, and through older ones too. Today, a theology that grew from rooms like that, and the power it talks about.

The name comes from Pentecost, the day in the book of Acts when the Holy Spirit comes on the disciples in Jerusalem. Before he leaves them, Jesus promises: "ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me." Then it happens. A sound like a rushing wind. Tongues like fire. The disciples speak, and visitors from far-off lands hear them in their own languages. Peter explains it with the prophet Joel: "your sons and your daughters shall prophesy." Pentecostal theology takes that day as a pattern, not only a memory. The Spirit, Pentecostals say, still comes with power: in worship, in healing, in gifts like speaking in tongues, and above all in boldness to tell others about Jesus. Notice the order in that promise. The power is for something: ye shall receive power, and ye shall be witnesses. It isn't for show. Experience matters deeply here. Faith is not only believed; it is met. That's part of why Pentecostal worship can be loud and open, with raised hands, spoken prayer and testimony. Christians differ on these gifts. Some hold that tongues and prophecy continue today. Others believe they belonged to the time of the apostles. Others welcome the Spirit's work in quieter ways. And Paul, writing to a church full of these gifts, puts something above them all: "Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal."

Bring to mind one person who's hard for you to love right now, and just hold them there, without forcing a warm feeling. If you pray, you can ask the Holy Spirit for power to love them, in your own words or with the old cry of the church, come, Holy Spirit; if you don't, ask what one loving act toward them would look like.
Pentecostal theology. A theology of the Holy Spirit, met in experience and giving power to witness, named for the day of Pentecost in Acts.
Your line: power to witness. Power for something, never for show. That's today, done.

1281.title: Newbigin's return
1281.hook: a missionary to India returns to Britain and sees the West as a mission field too
1281.howItsDone: Some congregations speak of their own neighborhood as their mission field, through hospitality, local service and simply being present; Newbigin's books are read by church leaders across traditions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pentecostal theology: the Spirit's power, given for a purpose. Your line was power to witness.

A young minister sits in South India, saying Tamil words aloud until they stick. He has sailed out from Britain as a missionary of the Church of Scotland, and he stays for years. He preaches in villages, and becomes a bishop in the Church of South India. Then, near the end of his working life, he comes home to Britain. And home looks strange to him. Thinner congregations. A culture that once called itself Christian, now living by other stories. Lesslie Newbigin looked hard at his own country and said it plainly: the West is a mission field too.
screen: `THE WEST IS A MISSION FIELD TOO.`

segments.voice: A missionary has to learn to see a culture from outside: what its people take for granted, what stories they live by, what they'd never think to question. Newbigin had done that for years in India. Back in Britain, he turned the same eyes on his own culture. He saw that the modern West had its own unquestioned beliefs, like any culture, and he thought Christians there had made too much peace with them without noticing. So he asked the missionary's question at home: how does the gospel sound here, to these neighbors? His answer had a surprising focus. Not mainly big campaigns: the local congregation. A congregation actually living the gospel, he wrote, in its worship, its care for neighbors and its life together, is how people come to understand the gospel at all. In John's Gospel, the risen Jesus says to his disciples: "as my Father hath sent me, even so send I you." Newbigin drew no line there between those who go far away and those who stay. For him, every disciple is sent, and home is where the sending starts. This week has walked through a house of many rooms: Rahner's ordinary, Schmemann's sacrament, Gutiérrez from below, Cone's cross, women's voices, Pentecostal power. And Newbigin, seeing his own front door with fresh eyes.

Picture the street where you live, and look at it the way a newcomer would, someone just arrived from far away: what do people here take for granted, what do they hope for and fear, and who is lonely? Don't judge it; just look. If you pray, you can hold your neighbors before God, one doorway at a time.
Newbigin's return. Lesslie Newbigin, home from India, seeing his own country as a mission field, and the local church as the place the gospel is explained by being lived.
Your line: home as mission. Every disciple is sent, starting from the front door. Back tomorrow, same hill.

chat.says: Mission means sending people overseas, right? What did Newbigin say about that?
options: He came home from India and said the West is a mission field too, and every disciple is sent.
He said mission is over now, since Britain already called itself a Christian country.
He said churches should stop meeting locally and put everything into big campaigns.
chat.meaning: Newbigin saw his own culture with a missionary's eyes, and said a congregation living the gospel is how people come to understand it. Every disciple is sent.
